summary:
Bahia is a state in north-east Brazil; the national framework applies, and the findings below are specific to the state.

The ANTRA 2025 dossier records 7 trans killings in Bahia during 2025, placing the state immediately behind the leading states, which recorded 8; a second report identifies those as Ceará and Minas Gerais. Across 1,261 killings recorded nationwide between 2017 and 2025, Bahia ranks third with 97, after São Paulo (151) and Ceará (107). These are raw counts with no per-capita denominator, and Bahia is one of Brazil's most populous states, so the ranking reflects population size as well as incidence and does not establish that the state is more dangerous per resident than smaller ones.

The pattern is not new. The ANTRA dossier for 2022 ranked Bahia seventh nationally for killings of trans people, with 7 killings of travestis in the state that year, when Pernambuco led the ranking.

On the weekend of 6-7 December 2025, Rhianna, an 18-year-old trans woman, was choked to death in Luís Eduardo Magalhães, in the west of the state. The Civil Police opened a feminicide investigation, treating the killing as gender-based. The suspect, a 19-year-old app driver, drove the victim's body to the police station, confessed and claimed self-defence, and was released.

Bahia was the first Brazilian state to enact an anti-discrimination ordinance, in 1997. On 1 June 2022 the Legislative Assembly passed, and on 30 June 2022 Assembly President Adolfo Menezes signed, the Millena Passos Law banning discrimination on grounds of gender identity; a parallel measure covering sexual orientation was signed the same day.

Transgender people in Bahia have been able to change their name and legal gender since 2008, with gender self-determination permitted since 2018, and the Bahia Public Defender's Office works with other agencies on joint efforts to facilitate document rectification. A decree signed by Governor Rui Costa on 23 May 2017 gave travesti and transexual people the right to use their social name and have their gender identity recognised across the state's direct and indirect public administration; the social name must appear alongside the legal name on official documents, and minors require guardian authorisation. On 11 May 2022 the Court of Justice of Bahia allowed a third gender option on documents, and on 26 December 2024 Governor Jerônimo Rodrigues sanctioned Law 14,806, exempting the cost of protest certificates so that document rectification is free of charge for transgender people.

In 2008 Léo Kret, a travesti club dancer, won a seat on the Salvador city council with 12,861 votes and, on taking office, insisted on a feminine wardrobe and on using the women's restroom.

Against these protections, on 17 December 2025 the Salvador City Council approved a bill banning the teaching of gender identity in schools, signed into law on 26 March 2026 by Mayor Bruno Soares Reis.
tangentialFactors:
Bahia sits in the top band of states in the annual trans-killing dossiers without leading it: third in the 2017-2025 cumulative count behind São Paulo and Ceará, and just behind Ceará and Minas Gerais in 2025. Its record combines a high raw count with early protective legislation, including the first state anti-discrimination ordinance in Brazil in 1997 and notarial recognition of marriages between people of the same sex from November 2012, ahead of nationwide recognition in 2013.

The state's protective measures and the capital's school restriction point in opposite directions: the Millena Passos Law and the 2017 social-name decree operate statewide, while the Salvador City Council's ban on teaching gender identity, signed in March 2026, applies within the capital's school system.

A homophobic attack on a teenager in Camaçari in 2022 drew national attention and prompted state authorities to act; the sources do not record it as trans-specific.
localsOnly:
Notaries in Bahia have recognised marriages between people of the same sex since 26 November 2012, before nationwide recognition. The homosexual stable union book is recognised by the National Institute of Social Security for inheritance sharing and pension receipt, with 30 reported legal cases in Bahia, including a surviving spouse receiving a pension after a companion's death. On 9 March 2010 a court in Salvador authorised the adoption of a child by a lesbian couple.

A preventative STD/AIDS programme for travesti sex workers in Bahia produced a booklet, folder and poster in realistic language and images, ran weekly safe-sex workshops, and recorded 900 interventions and the distribution of 14,400 condoms over six months.
outOfScopeNotes:
The ANTRA counts are raw totals; the sources provide no per-capita rate for Bahia or for the states it is compared with, so the ranking cannot be read as a measure of risk per resident.

No Bahia-specific rule, unit or documented case on the placement of trans prisoners in the state prison system appears in the sources; the national framework governs, and the state prison administration's practice is not documented here.

The 2004 list compiled by Grupo Gay da Bahia naming 159 murdered LGBTQ people is a national count and is not disaggregated to Bahia.

The effect of the Salvador school law on transgender students in the capital, and any legal challenge to it, is not yet documented.
